METADATA.title: Vintage Gibson ES-335 Value Guide: Prices By Year To 1979
METADATA.description: See vintage Gibson ES-335 values by year through 1979. Joe explains the era ranges, original parts, condition and case details behind each appraisal.
secondaryQueries: what is my Gibson ES-335 worth

OUTLINE: ## Asking Prices, Completed Sales And Offers
BODY:
Vintage Gibson ES-335 reference values run from $3,000 to $5,500 for typical 1970s examples to $33,000 to $70,000 for early dot-neck guitars, as of October 2026. I list every year from 1958 through 1979 below, with the finish, pickups and condition each range assumes.

For the year and originality checks behind that comparison, use my [Gibson ES-335 dating and authentication guide](/gibson-es-335-345-355-dating-guide/). This page focuses on the appraisal: which examples belong together, what changes the offer, and what information I need from an owner.

## Gibson ES-335 Values By Year

**As of October 2026. All ranges are in US dollars.** Each year is listed separately. **Repeated ranges are shared era references**, supported by at least three independent completed sales per comparison group, not three sales for every individual year. Match the condition notes below before applying a range.

| Year | Value Range | Comparison Group |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1958 | $33,000 to $70,000 | Dot Neck, Sunburst |
| 1959 | $33,000 to $70,000 | Dot Neck, Sunburst Or Cherry |
| 1960 | $33,000 to $70,000 | Dot Neck, Sunburst Or Cherry |
| 1961 | $33,000 to $70,000 | Dot Neck, Sunburst Or Cherry |
| 1962, Early Dot Neck | $33,000 to $70,000 | Shared Dot-Neck Reference |
| 1962, Block Neck | $25,000 to $37,000 | Block Neck, Original Humbuckers |
| 1963 | $25,000 to $37,000 | Block Neck, Original Humbuckers |
| 1964 | $25,000 to $37,000 | Block Neck, Original Humbuckers |
| 1965 | $13,000 to $15,500 | Factory Trapeze, Minor Changes |
| 1966 | $5,000 to $7,500 | Factory Trapeze, Played Originals |
| 1967 | $5,000 to $7,500 | Factory Trapeze, Played Originals |
| 1968 | $5,000 to $7,500 | Factory Trapeze, Played Originals |
| 1969 | $5,000 to $7,500 | Factory Trapeze, Played Originals |
| 1970 | $3,000 to $5,500 | Original Finish And Pickups |
| 1971 | $3,000 to $5,500 | Original Finish And Pickups |
| 1972 | $3,000 to $5,500 | Original Finish And Pickups |
| 1973 | $3,000 to $5,500 | Original Finish And Pickups |
| 1974 | $3,000 to $5,500 | Original Finish And Pickups |
| 1975 | $3,000 to $5,500 | Original Finish And Pickups |
| 1976 | $3,000 to $5,500 | Original Finish And Pickups |
| 1977 | $3,000 to $5,500 | Original Finish And Pickups |
| 1978 | $3,000 to $5,500 | Original Finish And Pickups |
| 1979 | $3,000 to $5,500 | Original Finish And Pickups |

The 1962 transition gets two rows because an early dot-neck example and a block-neck example need different comparisons. The 1965 range is for a factory trapeze guitar with minor changes; factory stopbars, other vibratos and untouched collector examples can require a different appraisal. The later trapeze and 1970s ranges include more playing wear than the clean early block-neck group.

Natural finishes, factory custom orders and modified stopbar guitars aren't priced as ordinary sunburst or cherry examples. A 1958 guitar also needs its own configuration checked before using the shared dot-neck reference. I don't treat these broad bands as a smooth price curve from one year to the next.

### Condition Behind The Ranges

**1958 To 1961 Dot-Neck Era:** Original sunburst or cherry finish and PAF pickups, no disclosed structural repair. Clean to lightly played; reproduction tuners can be present. Case completeness varies. Natural finishes excluded.

**1962 To 1964 Block-Neck Era:** Clean original-finish guitars with original humbuckers and no disclosed structural repair. Factory stopbar or vibrato, including unusually clean examples. Case completeness varies; minor replaced strap buttons accepted.

**1965 ES-335, Factory Trapeze, Cherry Or Sunburst:** Original finish and pickups, original case, no reported structural break. Minor changes allowed: replacement nut, period replacement tuners or a filled neck dent. This is not an all-original collector band.

**1966 To 1969 Trapeze Era:** Played original-finish guitars with original pickups and no disclosed structural repair. Replacement tuners or switch accepted; case can be replaced. Factory trapeze configuration.

**1970 To 1979 Standard ES-335TD:** Original-finish guitars with vintage Gibson pickups, no disclosed structural break, normal wear or minor hardware changes. Case originality varies. Stereo CRS, refinishes and replacement pickup sets excluded. Some lower-priced examples require minor control servicing; a fully functioning guitar should be compared accordingly.

I use rounded Reverb Price Guide final transaction prices and Heritage auction results, checked against the instrument descriptions. The records span 2020 to 2026, depending on the group; the review date doesn't turn an older sale into a current transaction. Auction totals include the buyer's premium. Shipping and tax are excluded, and these aren't dealer buying offers or guaranteed selling prices.

Seller descriptions supply the condition evidence behind these comparisons. I still need to examine the actual guitar before treating its finish, pickups or repair history as established. A repeated era range is a starting point for that appraisal, not a separate sale record for each year.


## The ES-335 Comparisons I Use

The ES-335 combines a solid center block with hollow sections on either side. It shares its broad outline with other Gibson models, but the model name still needs to be settled before any price comparison. An ES-345, an ES-355 and an ES-330 belong in their own appraisals.

My [ES-335, ES-345 and ES-355 comparison](/post/gibson-es-335-345-355-guide/) covers those family differences. Within the ES-335, I group guitars by the features a buyer is actually getting.

| Comparison Group | What I Match Before Comparing Prices |
| --- | --- |
| Early dot-neck examples | Year, finish, pickups, factory tailpiece and structural condition |
| Early block-neck examples | Original pickup combination, stopbar or factory vibrato, neck and finish |
| Mid-1960s examples | Factory tailpiece, neck dimensions, pickups and any later conversions |
| Later 1960s examples | Exact configuration, original finish, electronics and repair history |

A dot neck takes its name from the round fingerboard markers. Block neck refers to the rectangular markers used afterward. Those names are useful starting points, but I don't treat every guitar in either group as interchangeable.

[IMAGE 1]

### Early Dot-Neck Guitars

The early dot-neck period deserves its own comparison group. Original finish, original humbuckers and the factory tailpiece remain separate questions even when two examples have the same year on the listing. A sunburst guitar and a natural-finish guitar shouldn't be averaged together without accounting for the finish.

I also keep the condition of the neck and body in view. A handsome front photograph can leave a repaired headstock or heel outside the frame. An attractive example with a documented repair can be a useful player's guitar, but it isn't the same purchase as an unrepaired collector example.

For the detailed construction of that period, the [1959 ES-335 reference](/post/1959-gibson-es-335-authentication-guide/) shows one of the early guitars in my photo library. Its photographs are useful for understanding the configuration; they aren't sales records.

### Early Block-Neck Guitars

The transition to block inlays doesn't make all early block-neck ES-335s equal. The pickup combination, factory tailpiece, finish and condition still need to match the comparison. I want those details established before treating an early block-neck result as relevant to another guitar.

A pickup is the magnetic assembly beneath the strings that sends the signal to an amplifier. Early Gibson humbuckers include the PAF and Patent Number types, names taken from their labels. A price comparison needs the actual installed pickups and their condition, rather than a guess based on the year alone.

The [1962 ES-335 model guide](/post/1962-gibson-es-335-guide/) documents that transitional year. If a guitar's date or configuration remains uncertain, I leave the valuation conditional on resolving it.

[IMAGE 2]

### The Mid-1960s Transition

Factory stopbars, trapeze tailpieces and vibratos need different comparisons. A stopbar is the bar behind the bridge that anchors the strings. A trapeze anchors them from the end of the body, while a vibrato adds a moving mechanism that lets the player change pitch with an arm.

A later conversion can make a guitar look like a more sought-after factory configuration. It doesn't undo the conversion or restore the original factory specification. I evaluate the current guitar and its documented history together.

The [1965 ES-335 short Maestro example](/post/1965-gibson-es-335-short-maestro-vibrola/) illustrates why the exact hardware belongs in the description. A year alone doesn't tell a buyer which version is being offered.

[IMAGE 3]

### Later 1960s Examples

Later 1960s ES-335s need their own completed-sale comparisons. I don't price them by applying a guessed discount to a dot-neck range. That shortcut hides differences in necks, hardware, pickups and the actual condition of the examples being compared.

A clean later guitar can also present a different choice from an earlier guitar with substantial repairs. I describe those choices directly so an owner can understand why two broadly similar instruments might draw different offers.

The [1966 ES-335 reference](/post/1966-gibson-es-335-authentication-guide/) and [1968 ES-335 guide](/post/1968-gibson-es-335-guide/) cover those examples in detail. This value page uses that identification work without repeating the inspection procedure.

[IMAGE 4]

### The 1970s Reference

The 1970s rows cover ordinary ES-335 examples with original finish and pickups, allowing the minor hardware changes described above. The comparisons include walnut and sunburst guitars, and cases range from original to replacements. Some lower-priced examples need control servicing, so I don't describe the whole group as flawless.

Factory special versions and later conversions need their own comparisons. Original electronics, working controls and a clear repair history make the description more useful than the year alone.

## Original Finish And The Appraisal

Original finish is the coating applied when the guitar was built. A refinish replaces it; overspray adds finish over some or all of the existing surface. I keep those descriptions separate because they describe different histories.

Ordinary wear isn't the same thing as refinishing. A worn original guitar and a freshly refinished guitar may appeal to different buyers even when both play well. Photographs that show the whole instrument help keep the appraisal from being driven only by its most flattering angle.

I won't assign a blanket percentage to finish work without comparable evidence. The extent of the work, the guitar's other changes and the condition of the comparison instruments all affect the result. Applying several guessed discounts in sequence can produce a precise-looking figure with no reliable foundation.

Color also needs a careful description. A factory finish name is a claim about the instrument's history, while a photograph records how it looks under particular lighting. I don't infer a rare factory finish from a color cast in a photograph.

[IMAGE 5]

## Pickups, Electronics And Replacement Parts

For an ES-335, the installed pickup set is part of the instrument being valued. A modern replacement can work well musically without carrying the same collector appeal as the original set. If the original pickups remain in the case, I want that fact included in the appraisal record.

A rewound pickup also needs to be disclosed. Rewinding replaces the wire in the pickup coil; it isn't the same description as an untouched original pickup. I evaluate the instrument with the repair described, rather than treating the replacement wire as invisible because the cover looks old.

Small parts need the same precise language. A replacement bridge, changed tuners and missing knobs are separate changes, and their effects depend on the rest of the guitar. A reversible replacement with the original part retained is a different situation from work that removed wood or left extra holes.

I don't add the retail asking prices of loose vintage parts to estimate the guitar's total value. A complete instrument is a different purchase from a collection of components. That parts-total method can overstate the likely sale price and obscure structural or finish issues.

## Repairs, Frets And Playing Condition

A repaired headstock or neck joint belongs in the initial description. The repair's location, stability, appearance and documentation affect how I assess the guitar. Clear photographs and the repairer's invoice, if available, are more useful than the unexplained phrase repaired professionally.

A quality refret is accepted maintenance. It preserves the all-original classification of an otherwise all-original guitar, while taking it out of the museum-quality category. Neck reshaping is a different alteration and shouldn't be grouped with routine fret maintenance.

Playing condition also needs a clear account. Tell me about buzzing, intermittent output, a stiff control or a problem that appears only after the guitar has been played for a while. You don't need to diagnose the cause before describing the symptom.

I prefer to see the guitar before an owner authorizes cosmetic work solely to prepare it for sale. Repair costs aren't automatically recovered in the selling price. Keeping the present condition documented lets us discuss the instrument without losing evidence of what changed.

## Cases, Paperwork And Ownership Records

The case and accessories are part of the package offered to a buyer. I distinguish an original case from a later Gibson case and from a modern replacement. A case can be useful and protective without being the one that originally accompanied the instrument.

Keep receipts, repair records and any original accessories together. Paperwork can support the ownership history or explain a repair, but it doesn't make an unrelated replacement part original. I match each record to the guitar rather than treating a large stack of documents as proof by itself.

If a part was removed years ago, leave it with the guitar and explain what you know. I don't need an owner to reinstall it before the first appraisal. That avoids turning a straightforward condition report into another round of work.

[IMAGE 6]

## Asking Prices, Completed Sales And Offers

An asking price tells me what a seller hopes to receive. A realized price records a completed transaction. I use completed results to support a range and keep dealer advertisements as a separate check on what buyers are being asked to pay.

The terms behind a result need to be comparable too. An auction total can include a buyer's premium, while marketplace transaction records may exclude shipping and taxes. Those amounts shouldn't be mixed without recording what each one includes.

A retail sale price also isn't the same as the amount an owner receives after selling costs. If you're comparing offers, put the expected net proceeds, timing and obligations beside each other. A larger headline number can come with fees, work or uncertainty that the headline doesn't show.

I buy vintage Gibsons nationwide from my shop in Mesa, Arizona. My [Gibson selling page](/sell-my-gibson-guitar/) explains that process. An appraisal begins with the guitar's details; it doesn't require an owner to have already decided to sell.

[IMAGE 7]

## Getting A Useful ES-335 Appraisal

Start with clear photographs of the front, back and both sides of the headstock. Include the case, any loose parts and the paperwork you have. Add close-ups of known repairs or damage instead of trying to hide them in a distant photograph.

Tell me the year you believe it is, where that information came from, and what you know about changes. It's fine to say you don't know. An uncertain date is easier to work with than a confident description that accidentally combines details from different models.

You can request a [free appraisal of your Gibson ES-335](/free-appraisal/) with those photographs and notes. I'll use the instrument's actual configuration and condition to explain the next valuation step.

mainEntity.name: How Much Is A Vintage Gibson ES-335 Worth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Vintage Gibson ES-335 reference values run from $3,000 to $5,500 for typical 1970s examples to $33,000 to $70,000 for early dot-neck guitars, as of October 2026. I list every year from 1958 through 1979 below, with the finish, pickups and condition each range assumes.

mainEntity.name: Why Do Several Years Show The Same Value Range?

acceptedAnswer.text: The repeated figures are shared era references based on at least three independent completed sales per comparison group. They aren't separate statistical estimates for every year. I use the guitar's exact configuration, condition and originality to refine that starting range rather than inventing an annual premium.

mainEntity.name: What Condition Do The Price Ranges Assume?

acceptedAnswer.text: Read the condition notes for the applicable era. Some groups cover clean original guitars, while others allow normal playing wear, a quality refret or disclosed minor parts changes. Case originality also varies. A full refinish, structural repair or replacement pickup requires a different comparison.

mainEntity.name: Is A Dealer Offer The Same As The Published Range?

acceptedAnswer.text: It isn't. The table describes completed-sale comparisons before shipping and tax. A buying offer also accounts for the instrument's condition, selling costs, preparation and the dealer's margin. I explain an offer for the actual guitar rather than promising the top of a general range.

mainEntity.name: Does A Quality Refret Change The Collector Category?

acceptedAnswer.text: A quality refret is accepted maintenance and preserves the all-original classification of an otherwise all-original guitar. It takes the instrument out of the museum-quality category. Neck reshaping is a separate alteration.

IMAGE_LIST.shows: The dot inlays, covered pickups and stopbar are visible on this sunburst ES-335. Photo by Joe Dampt.
IMAGE_LIST.alt: Sunburst Gibson ES-335 with dot inlays, two covered pickups and a stopbar in a pink-lined case

IMAGE_LIST.shows: This 1962 ES-335 shows the block inlays and stopbar combination. Finish, pickups and condition still need to match the price comparison. Photo by Joe Dampt.
IMAGE_LIST.alt: Cherry ES-335 with block inlays, covered humbuckers and a stopbar in a yellow-lined case

IMAGE_LIST.shows: This 1965 ES-335 has the short Maestro arrangement. It should be compared with the same factory configuration. Photo by Joe Dampt.
IMAGE_LIST.alt: Sunburst ES-335 with a short Maestro vibrato and its arm fitted

IMAGE_LIST.shows: The trapeze tailpiece anchors the strings from the end of this 1966 ES-335. A stopbar conversion would change its appraisal description. Photo by Joe Dampt.
IMAGE_LIST.alt: Cherry ES-335 with two covered pickups, block inlays and a trapeze tailpiece

IMAGE_LIST.shows: This 1968 example shows a later 1960s configuration. I compare its era and condition separately from the early dot-neck guitars. Photo by Joe Dampt.
IMAGE_LIST.alt: Sunburst ES-335 with block inlays, trapeze tailpiece and black witch hat knobs

IMAGE_LIST.shows: Keep hang tags, instructions and the case key with the instrument. They help describe the complete package. Photo by Joe Dampt.
IMAGE_LIST.alt: Gibson hang tags, instruction sheets and a case key arranged on a black guitar case

IMAGE_LIST.shows: The case interior and maker's badge help document what accompanies the guitar. Case condition is part of the comparison. Photo by Joe Dampt.
IMAGE_LIST.alt: Pink-lined brown guitar case with a Stone Case Company badge beside an ES-335 headstock
